Everything fits in a 3D printed case : an Arduino Nano, the nRF24L01, the MPU6050 and 4 CR2025 coin cells.

And here it is in action :

Of course Bluetooth would have been simpler, but the point of the project was to build the whole communication chain ourselves. And having an Arduino that can pair with any Logitech dongle is quite fun.

The presentation we gave at the end of the project (in French) is here.

item.title: XTrem Kernel : my Own RTOS for ARM Cortex M3
item.description:
Tasks, priorities, semaphores, mutexes and a little shell, written from scratch for the mbed LPC1768

I wrote XTrem Kernel in 2015 and it has been sitting on my hard drive since then, so I just put it on GitHub : ronangaillard/xtremkernel.

I wanted to know what really happens inside a real time operating system, and the best way to know was to write one. In less than two months I wrote a multitask kernel for ARM Cortex M3 processors : thousands of lines of low level C and a few hundred lines of assembly. It runs on the NXP LPC17XX chips, so on the original mbed LPC1768 board.

The kernel

A SysTick interrupt every millisecond gives the kernel its heartbeat. The scheduler keeps one queue of runnable tasks per priority level, always runs the highest priority one, and does round robin between tasks of the same priority.

The context switch itself is a few lines of assembly in the PendSV handler, the lowest priority interrupt of the Cortex M3 : it saves the registers of the current task on its stack, switches the stack pointer, and restores the registers of the next one. The Cortex M3 port of TNKernel was a great help to understand how to do it.

On top of that the kernel provides what you expect from an RTOS :

  • tasks with priorities, created with their own stack, and sleep()
  • timers and timeouts
  • semaphores
  • mutexes, with priority inheritance : when a high priority task waits for a mutex, the task holding it temporarily gets its priority, so it can’t be blocked by a medium priority task

The screenshot above is the classic first test : two tasks printing on the serial port, task 1 more often than task 2.

A small computer

Once the kernel worked, I wanted to use it for something. So I added :

  • a basic shell (ls, mount, whoami, reboot…)
  • a PS/2 keyboard driver
  • a VGA output through a Gameduino board on the SPI bus, with an 8x8 font
  • SD card support, with the FatFs module to read files and navigate in folders

With the keyboard and the screen, the mbed became a small standalone computer, running my own OS.

The next steps were to load binaries from the SD card and run them as tasks, and to move the shell and the FAT support out of the kernel and load them as modules, UNIX style. The hardware specific code is well separated from the kernel core, so porting it to other ARM processors should be easy too.

item.title: A Lamp That Reacts to Music
item.description:
A CD spindle, RGB LEDs, an Arduino, and a beat detection algorithm running on my computer

I wanted a lamp that changes color on the beat of the music, whatever the song style and whatever the volume. Here it is :

The lamp

The lamp is an old CD spindle case, with RGB LEDs I soldered in bands inside. An Arduino in the lamp drives the LEDs, and listens to the computer on the USB port.

Detecting the beat

The hard part is on the computer side, in Processing. The program does an FFT of the sound to split it into frequency bands. For each band it computes two averages of the energy : a long term one and a short term one. When the short term average jumps above the long term one, that’s a beat. Since everything is relative to the long term average, it works with a quiet song as well as with a loud one, and with any style of music.

At each beat the computer sends a random color to the Arduino, and the lamp changes color.

item.title: Arduino as a PIC Programmer
item.description:
Burning Microchip PICs from USB with an Arduino Uno, a resistor and a 12V supply

Updates

  • [3 March 2012] New version of the C# program and of the Arduino firmware, it now works with many 16F PICs.
  • [May 2012] Other people built on it : a version for the PIC18F family and a programmer for PIC32. Each PIC family has its own programming protocol and I am a student with a lot of homework, so I can’t maintain it anymore.
  • [2016] More than 20,000 downloads !
  • [2020] Eight years later, people are still posting their PIC references in the forum thread, hoping theirs is supported.

PIC microcontrollers are everywhere, but programming them needs a dedicated programmer. The cheap ones use a serial or parallel port that no modern computer has anymore, and the USB ones are expensive. I had an Arduino, so I wondered : why not make it do the job ?

The circuit

A PIC is programmed through ICSP (In-Circuit Serial Programming) : a clock line, a data line, and 12V on the MCLR pin to put the chip in programming mode. The Arduino handles the clock and data, and the 12V comes from an external supply.

That’s all : pin 8 is the data line through a 330 Ω resistor, pin 9 the clock, and pins 4, 5 and 6 are tied together to power the PIC. I used a PIC 16F628, but it should work with most 16F PICs. One safety rule : always reset the Arduino before putting the 12V.

The firmware

The Arduino sketch bit-bangs the ICSP protocol described in the Microchip datasheets : a 6 bit command, then a 16 bit word for the data (a start bit, 14 bits of data and a stop bit). On the USB side it accepts simple one letter commands on the serial port :

s : start in High Voltage Programming mode (S for Low Voltage)
wXXXXXXXXXXXXXX : write a word at the location pointed by the program counter
i : increment the program counter
r : read the current location
e : erase the full program memory
R : reset the PIC (program counter back to 0)

Every command answers D when it is done.

The software

Typing words one by one in the serial monitor gets old fast, so I wrote a small C# program for Windows. It reads a .hex file, sends it word by word to the Arduino, writes the configuration word, and can read the program memory back to check it.

Screenshot : Nishant_Sood, the first one to try it on the forum

It’s still a first version, so check your PIC with a regular programmer if you can. The code, the C# program and the list of tested PICs are on the Arduino forum : if you try it with another PIC, tell me there so I can add it to the list !

item.title: MiniOS : an Arduino Talking to a Minitel
item.description:
A DIN plug, a resistor and an Arduino Mega to bring the good old French Minitel back to life

Updates

  • [16 April 2010] This project was featured on the Arduino blog : Minitel is not dead!
  • [20 December 2013] The photos were featured on TEXT-MODE, a blog about text graphics through the ages (ASCII, PETSCII, Teletext, mosaics…)

The Minitel is the French terminal that brought online services to millions of homes long before the Internet. Plenty of them still sleep in attics. They have a nice feature : a “péri-informatique” DIN socket at the back, which is just a serial port. So I plugged an Arduino into one and wrote MiniOS, a tiny OS for the Minitel.

The wiring

There is not much to it : a male DIN plug wired to the second serial port of an Arduino Mega, and a 4.7 kΩ resistor. The two LEDs are only there to show what is going on.

The Minitel speaks at 1200 bauds, with 7 data bits and an even parity bit. The Arduino serial library could not do that at the time, so I set the UART register directly before starting the port :

UCSR1C = B00100100; // 7 bits + parity bit
Serial1.begin(1200);

Drawing on the screen

Once connected, the Minitel behaves like a simple terminal : you send it text, and control codes to move the cursor, clear the screen or change the font. For example ESC followed by O makes the text double size, ESC H makes it blink and ESC ] inverts the background. The whole OS is just a few functions that print screens and wait for a key :

  • a boot screen, with a blinking “Appuyez sur une touche…” (press any key)
  • a menu, quite empty I admit
  • “Fakebook”, for fun
  • the credits

All the code (a single file) is in the forum thread.

What happened next

I posted it on the French Arduino forum and the Arduino blog picked it up the next day. Other people rebuilt it and ported it to the Duemilanove (replace Serial1 with Serial and UCSR1C with UCSR0C). They also mapped the keys of the keyboard and even added a speaker to play music. Not bad for a menu with two entries !
